frontHtml: Endocarditis in a person who injects drugs: most likely valve and organism?
backHtml: Tricuspid valve; Staphylococcus aureus.

frontHtml: How do viridans streptococci stick to a damaged valve?
backHtml: Extracellular dextran (glucan) binds the sterile platelet–fibrin nidus on injured endothelium.

frontHtml: S. gallolyticus (S. bovis) endocarditis: what else must you look for?
backHtml: Colonic adenoma or carcinoma: colonoscopy.

frontHtml: Osler nodes vs Janeway lesions: pain and mechanism?
backHtml: Osler: tender finger/toe-pad nodules, immune complexes. Janeway: painless palm/sole macules, septic microemboli.

frontHtml: Early prosthetic valve endocarditis: leading organism and key virulence factor?
backHtml: Coagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis); polysaccharide biofilm.

frontHtml: Two zoonotic or vector-borne causes of culture-negative endocarditis?
backHtml: Coxiella burnetii (inhaled from livestock birth products) and Bartonella (B. quintana from body lice; B. henselae from cats).

frontHtml: Name the HACEK organisms.
backHtml: Haemophilus (non-influenzae), Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella: fastidious oral gram-negative bacilli.

frontHtml: Classic virus of myocarditis and its structure?
backHtml: Coxsackievirus B: picornavirus, nonenveloped, positive-sense ssRNA.

frontHtml: Chronic Chagas disease: heart and gut findings?
backHtml: Dilated cardiomyopathy, apical aneurysm, RBBB + left anterior fascicular block; megaesophagus and megacolon.

frontHtml: Mechanism of syphilitic aortitis?
backHtml: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum → medial loss → ascending aortic aneurysm, aortic regurgitation, tree-bark intima.

frontHtml: Typical cardiac lesion of Lyme disease?
backHtml: AV block (can fluctuate from first-degree to complete), weeks after erythema migrans.

frontHtml: How does diphtheria cause myocarditis?
backHtml: Exotoxin ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2 and halts protein synthesis in myocytes.

frontHtml: Suspected endocarditis, stable patient: first step?
backHtml: Three sets of blood cultures from separate venipunctures before antibiotics.

frontHtml: When is TEE preferred over (or after) TTE in suspected endocarditis?
backHtml: Negative TTE with high suspicion, prosthetic valve or device, S. aureus bacteremia, suspected abscess or other complication.

frontHtml: MSSA endocarditis: drug of choice?
backHtml: An antistaphylococcal β-lactam (cefazolin, nafcillin or oxacillin); better than vancomycin.

frontHtml: Main indications for surgery in endocarditis?
backHtml: Heart failure from valve dysfunction; uncontrolled infection (abscess, heart block, persistent bacteremia); fungal or resistant organisms; large mobile vegetation with embolism.

frontHtml: Who gets endocarditis prophylaxis before dental work?
backHtml: Prosthetic valve or valve-repair material, prior IE, specific congenital heart disease, transplant with valvulopathy.

frontHtml: Usual dental endocarditis prophylaxis regimen?
backHtml: A single oral dose of amoxicillin 30–60 minutes before the procedure (clindamycin no longer advised).

frontHtml: Aortic valve endocarditis with a lengthening PR interval: what do you suspect?
backHtml: Perivalvular (root) abscess reaching the conduction system: TEE and surgery.

frontHtml: Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis: a common regimen that avoids aminoglycosides?
backHtml: Ampicillin plus ceftriaxone.

frontHtml: Best noninvasive test to confirm acute myocarditis?
backHtml: Cardiac MRI (edema, non-coronary late gadolinium enhancement).

frontHtml: Lyme carditis: who needs admission and IV ceftriaxone?
backHtml: Symptomatic patients, PR ≥ 300 ms, or second- or third-degree block.

frontHtml: Is a permanent pacemaker usually needed for Lyme carditis?
backHtml: No: the block usually resolves with antibiotics; use temporary pacing if unstable.

frontHtml: How is chronic Chagas infection diagnosed?
backHtml: Serology with two different IgG assays (smears only help in the acute phase).

frontHtml: Treatment of tertiary (non-neurologic) syphilis such as aortitis?
backHtml: Benzathine penicillin G IM weekly for 3 weeks (neurosyphilis needs IV aqueous penicillin G).

frontHtml: Mechanism of acute rheumatic fever?
backHtml: Molecular mimicry: anti–M protein antibodies and T cells cross-react with cardiac myosin and valve proteins (type II hypersensitivity).

frontHtml: Which group A strep infection triggers rheumatic fever?
backHtml: Pharyngitis only (skin infection can cause glomerulonephritis but not rheumatic fever).

frontHtml: What is an Aschoff body?
backHtml: Fibrinoid necrosis with lymphocytes and Anitschkow cells (wavy "caterpillar" chromatin): rheumatic carditis.

frontHtml: Acute vs chronic rheumatic valve lesion?
backHtml: Acute: mitral regurgitation (valvulitis). Chronic: mitral stenosis with fused commissures.

frontHtml: Usual cause of death in acute rheumatic fever?
backHtml: Myocarditis with heart failure.

frontHtml: Which rheumatic fever manifestation can appear months later and alone?
backHtml: Sydenham chorea.

frontHtml: Libman–Sacks vegetations: location and association?
backHtml: Small sterile vegetations on both surfaces of (usually mitral) leaflets; lupus and antiphospholipid antibodies.

frontHtml: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis: classic setting?
backHtml: Hypercoagulable state, especially mucin-producing adenocarcinoma (pancreas, lung); sterile vegetations that embolise.

frontHtml: Why does carcinoid heart disease spare the left heart?
backHtml: Lung monoamine oxidase degrades serotonin (unless bronchial primary or right-to-left shunt).

frontHtml: Valve lesions of carcinoid heart disease?
backHtml: Tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonic stenosis or regurgitation (fibrous endocardial plaques).

frontHtml: Kawasaki disease: vessel size and key complication?
backHtml: Medium vessels; coronary artery aneurysm.

frontHtml: Takayasu vs giant cell arteritis: how to tell apart?
backHtml: Both granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis; Takayasu in women under 40 (arch branches, pulseless), GCA over 50 (temporal, jaw claudication).

frontHtml: Steroid-sparing biologic in giant cell arteritis and its target?
backHtml: Tocilizumab: IL-6 receptor antibody.

frontHtml: Late aortic complication of giant cell arteritis?
backHtml: Thoracic aortic aneurysm (and dissection).

frontHtml: Dressler syndrome: timing and mechanism?
backHtml: Pericarditis 1–6 weeks after MI; autoimmune reaction to myocardial antigens.

frontHtml: Secondary prophylaxis drug after rheumatic fever?
backHtml: IM benzathine penicillin G every 4 weeks (every 3 weeks in high-risk settings).

frontHtml: Duration of rheumatic fever prophylaxis with residual valve disease?
backHtml: 10 years or until age 40, whichever is longer (sometimes lifelong).

frontHtml: Duration of rheumatic fever prophylaxis without carditis?
backHtml: 5 years or until age 21, whichever is longer.

frontHtml: Which test in every suspected rheumatic fever case detects silent carditis?
backHtml: Echocardiography with Doppler.

frontHtml: Anticoagulant for atrial fibrillation with moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis?
backHtml: Warfarin (vitamin K antagonist), not a DOAC.

frontHtml: Symptomatic mitral stenosis in pregnancy: first-line drug?
backHtml: A β<sub>1</sub>-selective blocker (e.g. metoprolol), plus a diuretic for congestion.

frontHtml: Criteria for complete Kawasaki disease?
backHtml: Fever ≥ 5 days + ≥ 4 of: bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, oral changes, polymorphous rash, extremity changes, cervical node ≥ 1.5 cm.

frontHtml: Initial treatment of Kawasaki disease?
backHtml: IVIG 2 g/kg single infusion + aspirin, ideally within 10 days of fever onset.

frontHtml: When is echocardiography done in Kawasaki disease?
backHtml: At diagnosis, at 1–2 weeks and at 4–6 weeks (more often if coronaries are abnormal).

frontHtml: After IVIG for Kawasaki disease, when can MMR and varicella be given?
backHtml: About 11 months later.

frontHtml: Why give inactivated (not live) influenza vaccine to a child on aspirin?
backHtml: Live vaccine is contraindicated with aspirin, and influenza on aspirin raises the risk of Reye syndrome.

frontHtml: Long-term anticoagulant in thrombotic antiphospholipid syndrome?
backHtml: Warfarin; DOACs are inferior in high-risk (triple-positive, arterial) APS.

frontHtml: Antithrombotic for nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis?
backHtml: Therapeutic heparin (LMWH or unfractionated).

frontHtml: First test for suspected carcinoid syndrome?
backHtml: 24-hour urine 5-HIAA (or plasma 5-HIAA).

frontHtml: Suspected GCA with visual symptoms: first step?
backHtml: High-dose glucocorticoids immediately; biopsy or ultrasound within 1–2 weeks.

frontHtml: Diagnostic test for suspected Takayasu arteritis?
backHtml: MR or CT angiography of the aorta and its branches.

frontHtml: Most common tumor involving the heart in adults?
backHtml: A metastasis (lung, breast, lymphoma/leukemia most often; melanoma has the highest rate relative to its frequency).

frontHtml: Most common primary cardiac tumor in adults, and its usual site?
backHtml: Myxoma; left atrium, on a stalk attached to the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis.

frontHtml: Histology of a cardiac myxoma?
backHtml: Stellate and spindle 'myxoma cells', often around small vessels, in an abundant mucopolysaccharide (myxoid) matrix with hemorrhage.

frontHtml: Which cytokine from a myxoma causes fever, weight loss, anemia and a high ESR?
backHtml: Interleukin-6.

frontHtml: Three ways a left atrial myxoma causes disease?
backHtml: Mitral orifice obstruction (positional dyspnea/syncope, diastolic 'plop'), systemic embolism, and IL-6 constitutional symptoms.

frontHtml: Gene and syndrome for familial myxomas with spotty pigmentation and endocrine overactivity?
backHtml: Carney complex, autosomal dominant; PRKAR1A (protein kinase A regulatory subunit 1A).

frontHtml: Most common primary cardiac tumor in children, and its syndrome?
backHtml: Rhabdomyoma (ventricular, often multiple), associated with tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2 → mTOR); usually regresses.

frontHtml: Most common primary malignant cardiac tumor in adults; site and markers?
backHtml: Angiosarcoma; right atrium; endothelial markers (CD31, ERG); hemorrhagic pericardial effusion.

frontHtml: Valve tumor of older adults that causes embolic stroke?
backHtml: Papillary fibroelastoma (often aortic valve): avascular fronds with an elastic core.

frontHtml: Best initial test for a suspected cardiac mass?
backHtml: Transthoracic echocardiography (TEE and cardiac MRI for detail and tissue characterization).

frontHtml: Treatment of a left atrial myxoma?
backHtml: Prompt surgical excision including the stalk and a cuff of septum; follow-up echocardiography for recurrence.

frontHtml: Left atrial mass in a patient with atrial fibrillation and mitral stenosis: most likely?
backHtml: Thrombus (left atrial appendage); it shrinks with anticoagulation, unlike a myxoma.

frontHtml: Management of asymptomatic, non-obstructive rhabdomyomas in an infant?
backHtml: Observation with serial echocardiography; most regress. Treat only obstruction or refractory arrhythmia. Evaluate for tuberous sclerosis.

frontHtml: When to excise a papillary fibroelastoma?
backHtml: When it has embolized, is mobile or is large; small immobile asymptomatic lesions can be followed.

frontHtml: Malignant pericardial effusion with tamponade: immediate step and step for recurrence?
backHtml: Urgent pericardiocentesis (send cytology); recurrence → pericardial window or extended catheter drainage.

frontHtml: Which ion current produces phase 0 of the ventricular myocyte action potential?
backHtml: Fast inward Na<sup>+</sup> current through voltage-gated Na<sup>+</sup> channels.

frontHtml: Which current carries the upstroke (phase 0) of SA and AV nodal cells?
backHtml: L-type Ca<sup>2+</sup> current (nodal cells have no fast Na<sup>+</sup>-driven upstroke).

frontHtml: What sets the intrinsic heart rate in the SA node?
backHtml: The slope of phase 4 diastolic depolarization, driven by the funny current I<sub>f</sub> (HCN channels) and T-type Ca<sup>2+</sup> current.

frontHtml: How do sympathetic and vagal inputs change SA node firing?
backHtml: β<sub>1</sub> (cAMP) steepens phase 4 → faster; M<sub>2</sub> opens K<sup>+</sup> channels and flattens phase 4 → slower.

frontHtml: Rank conduction velocity through cardiac tissues.
backHtml: Purkinje fibres (fastest) > atrial and ventricular muscle > AV node (slowest).

frontHtml: Normal PR and QRS durations?
Which coronary artery usually supplies the AV node, and what is the clinical link?
backHtml: The artery giving off the posterior descending artery (usually the right coronary artery); inferior MI often causes (usually transient) nodal block.

frontHtml: What is the vulnerable period of ventricular repolarization?
backHtml: The relative refractory period on the downslope of the T wave; a stimulus there (R on T) can start VF.

frontHtml: Class IA antiarrhythmics: ECG effect and signature toxicities?
backHtml: Longer QRS and QT; torsades; procainamide → drug-induced lupus; quinidine → cinchonism, diarrhea.

frontHtml: Why do class IB drugs (lidocaine) work best in ischemic tissue?
backHtml: They bind preferentially to depolarized/inactivated Na<sup>+</sup> channels and unbind rapidly from normal tissue.

frontHtml: Class IC drugs: key mechanism feature and main contraindication?
backHtml: Strong use-dependent Na<sup>+</sup> block (QRS widens at fast rates); avoid in structural or ischemic heart disease.

frontHtml: Main ECG effect of class II and IV antiarrhythmics?
backHtml: Slower AV nodal conduction → longer PR interval.

frontHtml: Class III drugs act on which current and which phase?
backHtml: Block K<sup>+</sup> efflux (I<sub>Kr</sub>) → longer phase 3 and QT.

frontHtml: Name six toxicities of amiodarone.
backHtml: Pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction (hypo or hyper), hepatotoxicity, corneal deposits/optic neuropathy, photosensitivity/blue-grey skin, bradycardia; also raises warfarin and digoxin levels.

frontHtml: Adenosine: receptor, ionic effect and what blunts it?
backHtml: A<sub>1</sub> receptor → more K<sup>+</sup> efflux, less Ca<sup>2+</sup> current in AV node; blunted by theophylline/caffeine, enhanced by dipyridamole.

frontHtml: Ivabradine: target and typical adverse effect?
backHtml: Blocks I<sub>f</sub> (HCN) in the SA node; luminous visual phenomena (phosphenes), bradycardia.

frontHtml: Mobitz I vs Mobitz II: PR pattern and level of block?
backHtml: Mobitz I: progressive PR lengthening, AV node, usually benign. Mobitz II: constant PR then dropped beat, infranodal, may progress.

frontHtml: Third-degree AV block: relationship of P waves and QRS complexes?
backHtml: None: atria and ventricles beat independently; atrial rate exceeds the escape rate.

frontHtml: Three conditions needed for re-entry?
backHtml: Two pathways with different conduction/refractoriness, unidirectional block in one, and enough slow conduction for recovery ahead of the wave.

frontHtml: Typical atrial flutter: circuit and ablation target?
backHtml: Macro-re-entry around the tricuspid annulus (right atrium); ablate the cavotricuspid isthmus.

frontHtml: ECG triad of ventricular pre-excitation?
backHtml: Short PR, delta wave, slightly wide QRS.

frontHtml: Why is AF dangerous in WPW?
backHtml: The accessory pathway lacks the AV node's rate limiting, so very fast ventricular rates can degenerate to VF.

frontHtml: Long QT types 1, 2 and 3: channel and trigger?
backHtml: LQT1: ↓I<sub>Ks</sub>, exercise/swimming; LQT2: ↓I<sub>Kr</sub>, sudden noise/postpartum; LQT3: ↑late Na<sup>+</sup> current, rest/sleep.

frontHtml: Long QT plus congenital sensorineural deafness, recessive inheritance?
backHtml: Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome (I<sub>Ks</sub> channel subunits).

frontHtml: Brugada syndrome: ECG and treatment for high-risk patients?
backHtml: Coved ST elevation in V1–V2 (Na<sup>+</sup> channel loss of function); ICD.

frontHtml: First decision in any tachycardia?
backHtml: Is the patient unstable (hypotension, altered mentation, shock, ischemic pain, acute HF)? If so → synchronized cardioversion.

frontHtml: Stable paroxysmal SVT: sequence of treatment?
backHtml: Vagal maneuvers → IV adenosine → IV diltiazem/verapamil or β-blocker → cardioversion; ablation for recurrence.

frontHtml: Components of CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc?
backHtml: CHF 1, HTN 1, age ≥ 75 2, diabetes 1, stroke/TIA/embolism 2, vascular disease 1, age 65–74 1, female sex 1.

frontHtml: When must AF be anticoagulated with warfarin rather than a DOAC?
backHtml: Mechanical heart valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis.

frontHtml: Before elective cardioversion of AF ≥ 48 h, what is required?
backHtml: ≥ 3 weeks of anticoagulation or TEE excluding left atrial thrombus; anticoagulate ≥ 4 weeks afterwards.

frontHtml: Rate-control drug to avoid in AF with HFrEF?
backHtml: Diltiazem/verapamil (negative inotropes); use a β-blocker, with digoxin as an add-on.

frontHtml: Stable regular wide-complex tachycardia in a patient with prior MI: presumed diagnosis and drug options?
backHtml: VT; IV amiodarone or procainamide, or elective synchronized cardioversion. Never a calcium channel blocker.

frontHtml: Pre-excited AF (WPW), stable: treatment, and drugs to avoid?
backHtml: IV procainamide or ibutilide; avoid adenosine, β-blockers, diltiazem/verapamil, digoxin (and IV amiodarone).

frontHtml: Torsades de pointes with a pulse: first treatment?
backHtml: IV magnesium sulfate; stop QT-prolonging drugs, correct K<sup>+</sup> and Mg<sup>2+</sup>; defibrillate if pulseless.

frontHtml: Multifocal atrial tachycardia: ECG and main association?
backHtml: ≥ 3 P-wave morphologies with an irregular rate > 100/min; severe lung disease such as COPD. Treat the underlying cause.

frontHtml: Symptomatic bradycardia unresponsive to atropine: next step?
backHtml: Transcutaneous pacing or dopamine/epinephrine infusion, then transvenous pacing.

frontHtml: Which AV blocks need a permanent pacemaker even without symptoms (no reversible cause)?
backHtml: Mobitz II, advanced (high-grade) and third-degree AV block; alternating bundle branch block.

frontHtml: Reversible causes to exclude before pacing for bradycardia?
backHtml: AV nodal drugs, hyperkalemia, hypothyroidism, acute inferior MI, Lyme carditis, high vagal tone/sleep apnea.

frontHtml: Tachy–brady syndrome: why pace first?
backHtml: The rate-controlling drugs needed for the tachycardia would worsen the pauses.

frontHtml: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity: diagnostic criteria with massage?
backHtml: Pause ≥ 3 s (cardioinhibitory) and/or systolic fall ≥ 50 mm Hg (vasodepressor); pace recurrent cardioinhibitory syncope.

frontHtml: RBBB vs LBBB in V1?
backHtml: RBBB: rsR′ (M-shaped) in V1. LBBB: deep broad S in V1 with broad notched R in V6.

frontHtml: Pacing spikes not followed by a QRS?
backHtml: Failure to capture (lead dislodgement, fracture, high threshold, hyperkalemia, battery).

frontHtml: Spikes appearing on top of the patient's own QRS complexes?
backHtml: Failure to sense (undersensing).

frontHtml: What does a magnet do to a pacemaker?
backHtml: Switches it to asynchronous pacing at a fixed rate (useful with electrocautery or oversensing).

frontHtml: Shockable vs nonshockable arrest rhythms?
backHtml: Shockable: VF, pulseless VT. Nonshockable: PEA, asystole.

frontHtml: Timing of epinephrine and amiodarone in VF arrest?
backHtml: Epinephrine after the 2nd shock then every 3–5 min; amiodarone (or lidocaine) after the 3rd shock.

frontHtml: PEA/asystole: first drug and key search?
backHtml: Epinephrine as soon as possible; search for reversible causes (Hs and Ts).

frontHtml: List the reversible causes of cardiac arrest.
backHtml: Hypovolemia, hypoxia, acidosis, hypo/hyperkalemia, hypothermia; tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, coronary or pulmonary thrombosis.

frontHtml: High-quality CPR targets?
backHtml: 100–120 compressions/min, ≥ 5 cm depth, full recoil, minimal interruptions, 30:2 without an advanced airway.

frontHtml: ROSC with ST elevation on the ECG?
backHtml: Emergent coronary angiography, even if comatose.

frontHtml: Primary prevention ICD criteria?
backHtml: LVEF ≤ 35%, NYHA II–III despite ≥ 3 months of optimal therapy (≥ 40 days after MI), reasonable survival.

frontHtml: Congenital long QT: first-line drug?
backHtml: Nonselective β-blocker (nadolol or propranolol), plus avoiding QT-prolonging drugs; ICD after arrest.

frontHtml: On a pressure–volume loop, what does systolic dysfunction do to the end-systolic pressure–volume line and the loop?
backHtml: The line flattens (lower contractility); end-systolic and end-diastolic volumes rise, so the loop shifts right and the ejection fraction falls.

frontHtml: Diastolic dysfunction: which pressure–volume relation changes and how?
backHtml: The end-diastolic pressure–volume curve becomes steeper: a normal filling volume costs a high end-diastolic pressure.

frontHtml: Where and why is BNP secreted?
backHtml: From ventricular myocytes, in response to wall stretch (volume or pressure overload). It raises cGMP to cause natriuresis and vasodilation.

frontHtml: Which enzyme breaks down natriuretic peptides and bradykinin, and what drug inhibits it?
backHtml: Neprilysin; sacubitril (given with valsartan, never with an ACE inhibitor).

frontHtml: Cor pulmonale: definition and main mechanism?
backHtml: Right ventricular hypertrophy or failure caused by lung or pulmonary vascular disease; chiefly hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction raising RV afterload.

frontHtml: Name five causes of high-output heart failure.
backHtml: Thyrotoxicosis, severe anemia, arteriovenous fistula, wet beriberi (thiamine deficiency), Paget disease of bone (also pregnancy, sepsis, cirrhosis).

frontHtml: Why is the murmur of acute severe mitral regurgitation often soft?
backHtml: The small non-compliant left atrium's pressure rises quickly (giant v wave), so the LV–LA gradient falls early in systole.

frontHtml: S3 versus S4: which suggests a dilated volume-overloaded ventricle and which a stiff one?
backHtml: S3: dilated, volume-overloaded (systolic failure). S4: stiff, hypertrophied (diastolic dysfunction); an S4 is never normal.

frontHtml: The four drug classes that lower mortality in HFrEF?
backHtml: ARNI (or ACE inhibitor/ARB), evidence-based beta-blocker (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol), mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, SGLT2 inhibitor.

frontHtml: Ejection fraction cut-offs for HFrEF, HFmrEF and HFpEF?
backHtml: HFrEF ≤ 40%; HFmrEF 41–49%; HFpEF ≥ 50%.

frontHtml: When should an MRA not be started in HFrEF?
backHtml: Potassium ≥ 5.0 mEq/L or eGFR ≤ 30 mL/min/1.73 m²; hold or reduce it if potassium rises above 5.5 mEq/L.

frontHtml: Which patients with HFrEF benefit from hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate?
backHtml: Self-identified Black patients with NYHA III–IV symptoms on optimal therapy, and anyone unable to take any renin–angiotensin blocker.

frontHtml: Primary-prevention ICD criteria in HFrEF?
backHtml: EF ≤ 35%, NYHA II–III despite ≥ 3 months of guideline therapy, > 40 days after MI, expected survival > 1 year.

frontHtml: Cardiac resynchronisation therapy: who benefits most?
backHtml: EF ≤ 35%, sinus rhythm, left bundle branch block with QRS ≥ 150 ms, symptomatic despite guideline therapy.

frontHtml: Which drug classes worsen HFrEF?
backHtml: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, thiazolidinediones, NSAIDs, cilostazol and most class I antiarrhythmics.

frontHtml: Which drug class reduces HF hospitalisation in HFpEF?
backHtml: SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin); diuretics treat congestion.

frontHtml: Hypertensive acute pulmonary edema in an alert patient: first treatments?
backHtml: Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation, high-dose nitroglycerin and an IV loop diuretic.

frontHtml: 'Cold and wet' decompensated heart failure: what drug class?
backHtml: An inotrope (dobutamine or milrinone) plus diuretic; norepinephrine if hypotensive.

frontHtml: Cardiogenic shock after acute MI: what treatment improves survival?
backHtml: Emergency revascularisation of the culprit artery (usually PCI).

frontHtml: Why follow NT-proBNP rather than BNP in a patient on sacubitril–valsartan?
backHtml: Neprilysin inhibition raises BNP itself; NT-proBNP is not a neprilysin substrate.

frontHtml: Why is the subendocardium the layer most vulnerable to ischemia?
backHtml: It is furthest from the epicardial arteries and most compressed during systole; LV flow occurs mainly in diastole.

frontHtml: ST elevation in II, III and aVF: territory and usual culprit artery?
backHtml: Inferior wall; right coronary artery (left circumflex in left-dominant hearts).

frontHtml: ST elevation in V1–V4: which artery?
backHtml: Left anterior descending (anterior and septal wall).

frontHtml: How does a posterior MI look on a standard 12-lead ECG?
backHtml: ST depression with tall R waves in V1–V3; confirm with ST elevation in V7–V9.

frontHtml: Troponin kinetics after MI?
backHtml: Rises within hours, peaks at about 24 hours, stays raised 7–10 days.

frontHtml: Why was CK-MB used to detect reinfarction?
backHtml: It returns to normal within 2–3 days, so a new rise means new necrosis.

frontHtml: Dominant microscopic finding 1–3 days after MI?
backHtml: Neutrophil infiltration of coagulation necrosis (clinically: early fibrinous pericarditis).

frontHtml: When after MI is the wall weakest, and what complications occur then?
backHtml: About days 3–14 (macrophage phase, before collagen): free wall, septal or papillary muscle rupture.

frontHtml: What causes contraction band necrosis?
backHtml: Reperfusion of lethally injured myocytes: calcium influx causes hypercontraction.

frontHtml: Features of a rupture-prone plaque?
backHtml: Thin fibrous cap, large lipid-rich necrotic core, many macrophages (MMPs degrade the cap).

frontHtml: Main mechanism by which nitrates relieve exertional angina?
backHtml: Venodilation → lower preload → smaller LV volume and wall stress → less oxygen demand.

frontHtml: Clopidogrel versus ticagrelor: activation and binding?
backHtml: Clopidogrel: prodrug activated by CYP2C19, irreversible. Ticagrelor: active drug, reversible, can cause dyspnea.

frontHtml: Which P2Y12 inhibitor is avoided after stroke or TIA?
backHtml: Prasugrel.

frontHtml: Mechanism of ranolazine?
backHtml: Inhibits the late inward sodium current, reducing calcium overload and diastolic wall tension; can prolong QT.

frontHtml: What is coronary steal in vasodilator stress testing?
backHtml: Normal arterioles dilate while those beyond a stenosis are already maximal, so flow shifts away from the stenotic region.

frontHtml: Why is a non-selective beta-blocker avoided in vasospastic angina?
backHtml: Unopposed α-adrenergic vasoconstriction can worsen spasm; use a calcium channel blocker.

frontHtml: Best stress test for a patient with LBBB?
backHtml: Vasodilator (regadenoson or adenosine) myocardial perfusion imaging.

frontHtml: First-line daily antianginal drugs in chronic coronary disease?
backHtml: A beta-blocker or a calcium channel blocker, plus sublingual nitroglycerin as needed.

frontHtml: When is coronary bypass surgery favoured over PCI in stable disease?
backHtml: Significant left main disease, or multivessel disease with diabetes or reduced EF.

frontHtml: Nitrate timing after PDE-5 inhibitors?
backHtml: Avoid for 24 hours after sildenafil or vardenafil and 48 hours after tadalafil.

frontHtml: STEMI: preferred reperfusion and time targets?
backHtml: Primary PCI within 90 minutes of first contact (120 minutes if transfer needed); otherwise fibrinolysis within 30 minutes of arrival.

frontHtml: Is fibrinolysis used in NSTEMI?
backHtml: No: no benefit without complete occlusion, more bleeding.

frontHtml: NSTE-ACS: indications for immediate (< 2 h) angiography?
backHtml: Refractory angina, hemodynamic instability, acute heart failure, sustained ventricular arrhythmias, mechanical complications.

frontHtml: Inferior STEMI with hypotension, raised JVP and clear lungs: diagnosis and treatment?
backHtml: Right ventricular infarction: IV fluids, urgent reperfusion; avoid nitrates and diuretics.

frontHtml: Default duration of DAPT after ACS treated with a stent?
backHtml: 12 months (shorter with high bleeding risk), then lifelong single antiplatelet therapy.

frontHtml: After ACS, LDL ≥ 70 mg/dL on a maximal statin: next drug?
backHtml: Ezetimibe; then a PCSK9 inhibitor if still above goal.

frontHtml: Dilated cardiomyopathy: which phase of the cardiac cycle fails, and which hypertrophy pattern is seen?
backHtml: Systolic dysfunction (low ejection fraction) with eccentric hypertrophy (sarcomeres added in series).

frontHtml: Most common genetic cause of familial dilated cardiomyopathy?
backHtml: Truncating variants in TTN (titin); inheritance is usually autosomal dominant.

frontHtml: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: inheritance, two most often affected genes and histologic hallmark?
backHtml: Autosomal dominant; MYH7 (β-myosin heavy chain) and MYBPC3 (myosin-binding protein C); myocyte disarray.

frontHtml: Which manoeuvres make the murmur of obstructive HCM louder?
backHtml: Those that shrink the left ventricle: Valsalva strain, standing up, vasodilators (nitrates, amyl nitrite), dehydration.

frontHtml: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy: typical patient, trigger and angiographic finding?
backHtml: Postmenopausal woman after acute emotional or physical stress; ACS-like presentation with apical ballooning and no obstructive coronary disease.

frontHtml: Cardiac amyloidosis: what ECG–echo mismatch is classic?
backHtml: Thick ventricular walls on echocardiography with low QRS voltage on the ECG.

frontHtml: Pressure overload versus volume overload: how do myocytes respond?
backHtml: Pressure overload → sarcomeres in parallel (concentric hypertrophy). Volume overload → sarcomeres in series (eccentric hypertrophy).

frontHtml: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy: pathology?
backHtml: Fibrofatty replacement of (mainly right) ventricular myocardium, usually from desmosomal gene variants; ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death in the young.

frontHtml: Biopsy hallmark of viral myocarditis?
backHtml: Lymphocytic infiltrate with adjacent myocyte necrosis.

frontHtml: Why does the posteromedial papillary muscle rupture more often than the anterolateral?
backHtml: It usually has a single supply (posterior descending artery), whereas the anterolateral muscle is supplied by both the LAD and the circumflex.

frontHtml: When after MI is the risk of free wall, septal and papillary muscle rupture highest, and why?
backHtml: Roughly days 3–14: macrophages have removed necrotic myocytes but collagen has not yet formed, so the wall is weakest.

frontHtml: Post-MI new holosystolic murmur with a thrill at the left lower sternal border and an O<sub>2</sub> step-up in the right ventricle?
backHtml: Ventricular septal rupture.

frontHtml: True ventricular aneurysm versus pseudoaneurysm?
backHtml: True: thin scarred wall, wide neck, weeks to months after MI, low rupture risk. Pseudoaneurysm: contained rupture walled off by pericardium, narrow neck, high rupture risk.

frontHtml: Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy: classic findings?
backHtml: Dilated cardiomyopathy with an apical aneurysm, right bundle branch block ± left anterior fascicular block, and megaesophagus/megacolon.

frontHtml: First-line drug for symptomatic obstructive HCM?
backHtml: A non-vasodilating β-blocker (non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker if β-blockers fail or are not tolerated).

frontHtml: Drugs to avoid in obstructive HCM?
backHtml: Arterial vasodilators (dihydropyridines, nitrates), aggressive diuretics and digoxin: all shrink the ventricle or raise contractility and worsen obstruction.

frontHtml: HCM: indications for an ICD (examples)?
backHtml: Prior cardiac arrest or sustained VT; primary prevention with risk markers such as unexplained syncope, sudden death in a close relative, wall thickness ≥30 mm, apical aneurysm, LVEF <50% or extensive late gadolinium enhancement.

frontHtml: Suspected cardiac amyloidosis: what must be excluded before a bone-tracer scan can diagnose ATTR?
backHtml: A monoclonal protein (serum free light chains plus serum and urine immunofixation), to exclude AL amyloidosis.

frontHtml: Disease-modifying therapy for ATTR cardiomyopathy?
backHtml: A transthyretin stabiliser such as tafamidis.

frontHtml: Alcoholic cardiomyopathy: intervention most likely to restore ejection fraction?
backHtml: Complete abstinence from alcohol, together with guideline-directed HFrEF therapy.

frontHtml: Post-MI papillary muscle rupture with shock: management?
backHtml: Urgent echocardiography, afterload reduction and temporary mechanical support as a bridge to emergency mitral valve surgery.

frontHtml: Right ventricular infarction: what to give and what to avoid?
backHtml: Give IV fluids (inotropes if needed) and reperfuse; avoid nitrates, diuretics and morphine (preload-dependent).

frontHtml: Left ventricular thrombus after anterior MI: treatment?
backHtml: Oral anticoagulation for about 3 months, then repeat imaging.

frontHtml: Return to competitive sport after myocarditis?
backHtml: Avoid competitive sport for about 3–6 months, then return only after normal ECG, echocardiography, rhythm monitoring and exercise testing.

frontHtml: Immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis: management?
backHtml: Stop the drug and give high-dose glucocorticoids; monitor closely for arrhythmias and heart block.

frontHtml: ECG of acute pericarditis?
backHtml: Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression; aVR shows PR elevation and ST depression; no Q waves or territorial reciprocal changes.

frontHtml: Why does pericardial pain radiate to the trapezius ridge?
backHtml: The parietal pericardium is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5).

frontHtml: Beck triad?
backHtml: Hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure and muffled heart sounds: cardiac tamponade.

frontHtml: Mechanism of pulsus paradoxus in tamponade?
backHtml: Inspiration increases right ventricular filling; in a fixed pericardial volume the septum bows into the LV, lowering LV filling and stroke volume (ventricular interdependence).

frontHtml: Jugular venous y descent: tamponade versus constriction?
backHtml: Tamponade: blunted or absent. Constriction: prominent and steep.

frontHtml: Electrical alternans?
backHtml: Beat-to-beat alternation of QRS amplitude as the heart swings in a large pericardial effusion; suggests tamponade.

frontHtml: Pericardial knock: what is it?
backHtml: An early diastolic sound in constrictive pericarditis from abrupt cessation of ventricular filling by the rigid pericardium.

frontHtml: Pericarditis 1–3 days versus weeks after MI?
backHtml: 1–3 days: fibrinous inflammation over a transmural infarct. Weeks: autoimmune post-cardiac injury (Dressler) syndrome.

frontHtml: Type of pericarditis typical of uremia and transmural MI?
backHtml: Fibrinous.

frontHtml: Main cause of constrictive pericarditis worldwide, and in high-income countries?
backHtml: Tuberculosis worldwide; prior cardiac surgery, mediastinal radiation and idiopathic or viral pericarditis in high-income countries.

frontHtml: First-line treatment of uncomplicated acute pericarditis?
backHtml: High-dose NSAID or aspirin (tapered) plus colchicine for about 3 months, as an outpatient.

frontHtml: High-risk features that require admission in acute pericarditis?
backHtml: Fever >38 °C, subacute onset, large effusion or tamponade, failure of NSAIDs after a week, immunosuppression, trauma, oral anticoagulation, raised troponin (myopericarditis).

frontHtml: Anti-inflammatory of choice for pericarditis after MI?
backHtml: Aspirin; avoid other NSAIDs and glucocorticoids because they may impair infarct healing.

frontHtml: Echocardiographic signs of tamponade?
backHtml: Right atrial systolic collapse, right ventricular diastolic collapse, plethoric IVC and exaggerated respiratory variation in inflow.

frontHtml: What to avoid before draining tamponade?
backHtml: Diuretics, vasodilators and (when possible) intubation with positive-pressure ventilation.

frontHtml: Uremic pericarditis without tamponade: treatment?
backHtml: Start or intensify dialysis.

frontHtml: Recurrent malignant pericardial effusion: treatment?
backHtml: Pericardial window (or extended catheter drainage) plus treatment of the cancer.

frontHtml: Definitive treatment of chronic symptomatic constrictive pericarditis?
backHtml: Surgical pericardiectomy.

frontHtml: Why are glucocorticoids second line in acute pericarditis?
backHtml: Early steroid use increases the risk of recurrence; reserve them for NSAID/colchicine failure or contraindication, or specific indications.

frontHtml: Aortic stenosis murmur and associated pulse?
backHtml: Crescendo–decrescendo systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids; slow-rising, weak pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus).

frontHtml: Most common cause of aortic stenosis in older adults, and the type of calcification?
backHtml: Age-related calcific degeneration of a trileaflet valve; dystrophic calcification with normal serum calcium.

frontHtml: Genetic syndrome associated with bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation?
backHtml: Turner syndrome (45,X).

frontHtml: Mitral valve prolapse: effect of standing on the click?
backHtml: Smaller LV volume → the click occurs earlier and the murmur lasts longer.

frontHtml: Mitral stenosis: what does a short S2–opening snap interval mean?
backHtml: Higher left atrial pressure, i.e. more severe stenosis.

frontHtml: Why does tachycardia worsen mitral stenosis?
backHtml: It shortens diastole, leaving less time for the atrium to empty across the narrow valve, so the gradient and left atrial pressure rise.

frontHtml: Chronic aortic regurgitation: pulse findings and mechanism?
backHtml: Wide pulse pressure with bounding, collapsing pulses: a large stroke volume plus diastolic runoff into the LV.

frontHtml: Rheumatic heart disease: immune mechanism and pathognomonic lesion?
backHtml: Molecular mimicry (type II hypersensitivity) against streptococcal M protein; Aschoff bodies with Anitschkow cells.

frontHtml: Why does carcinoid heart disease spare the left-sided valves?
backHtml: Lung monoamine oxidase inactivates serotonin before blood reaches the left heart.

frontHtml: Heyde syndrome?
backHtml: Severe aortic stenosis with GI angiodysplasia bleeding from acquired von Willebrand syndrome (shear-induced loss of large vWF multimers).

frontHtml: Which murmurs get louder with sustained handgrip?
backHtml: Mitral regurgitation, aortic regurgitation and VSD (higher afterload); aortic stenosis and HCM murmurs soften.

frontHtml: Which murmurs always need echocardiography?
backHtml: Any diastolic or continuous murmur, any murmur grade ≥3, and any murmur with symptoms or abnormal findings.

frontHtml: Echocardiographic criteria for severe aortic stenosis?
backHtml: Peak velocity ≥4 m/s, mean gradient ≥40 mm Hg, valve area ≤1.0 cm<sup>2</sup>.

frontHtml: Indications for valve replacement in severe aortic stenosis?
backHtml: Symptoms; or no symptoms with LVEF <50%; or other cardiac surgery planned.

frontHtml: TAVR or SAVR?
backHtml: Heart team decision: TAVR favoured in older or higher-risk patients with suitable access; SAVR in younger, lower-risk patients.

frontHtml: Asymptomatic severe primary mitral regurgitation: when to operate?
backHtml: When the LV shows dysfunction (EF ≤60% or end-systolic diameter ≥40 mm); repair preferred over replacement.

frontHtml: Acute severe aortic regurgitation: treatment and what to avoid?
backHtml: Urgent surgery; avoid an intra-aortic balloon pump and β-blockade.

frontHtml: Anticoagulant for a mechanical heart valve?
backHtml: Warfarin for life; DOACs are contraindicated.

frontHtml: Atrial fibrillation with moderate or severe rheumatic mitral stenosis: anticoagulant?
backHtml: Warfarin, regardless of the CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc score; not a DOAC.

frontHtml: Who needs endocarditis prophylaxis before gingival dental procedures?
backHtml: Prosthetic valves (including transcatheter), prosthetic material used in valve repair, prior endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease and transplant valvulopathy.

frontHtml: Symptomatic mitral stenosis in pregnancy: first-line drug?
backHtml: A β<sub>1</sub>-selective blocker (e.g. metoprolol) to slow the heart, with cautious diuresis.

frontHtml: Definition of orthostatic hypotension?
backHtml: A sustained fall of ≥ 20 mm Hg systolic or ≥ 10 mm Hg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing (or head-up tilt).

frontHtml: Afferent nerve from the carotid sinus baroreceptors?
backHtml: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX); the aortic arch afferents travel in the vagus (CN X).

frontHtml: Heart-rate clue to neurogenic orthostatic hypotension?
backHtml: Little heart-rate rise: ratio of heart-rate rise to systolic fall below about 0.5 beats/min per mm Hg.

frontHtml: Multiple system atrophy histology?
backHtml: α-Synuclein glial cytoplasmic inclusions in oligodendrocytes.

frontHtml: Midodrine: mechanism and main adverse effect?
backHtml: Prodrug of a peripheral α<sub>1</sub> agonist; supine hypertension (also piloerection, urinary retention).

frontHtml: Droxidopa is converted to norepinephrine by which enzyme?
backHtml: Aromatic L-amino acid (DOPA) decarboxylase.

frontHtml: Fludrocortisone electrolyte effect?
backHtml: Hypokalemia (mineralocorticoid-driven K<sup>+</sup> secretion), with sodium and water retention.

frontHtml: Why does primary, but not secondary, adrenal insufficiency cause hyperkalemia?
backHtml: Primary destroys the zona glomerulosa (no aldosterone); secondary loses only ACTH, and aldosterone is controlled by angiotensin II.

frontHtml: Three age-related changes that promote orthostatic hypotension?
backHtml: Reduced baroreflex sensitivity, blunted β-adrenergic responses, and lower renin/aldosterone and thirst (plus a preload-dependent stiff ventricle).

frontHtml: How are orthostatic vital signs measured?
backHtml: After 5 minutes supine, then at 1 and 3 minutes of standing; record both pressure and pulse.

frontHtml: Three parts of the initial evaluation of every syncope?
backHtml: History (with witness), physical examination including orthostatic vital signs, and a 12-lead ECG.

frontHtml: POTS criteria?
backHtml: Heart-rate rise ≥ 30/min (≥ 40/min at 12–19 years) within 10 minutes of standing, with symptoms, without orthostatic hypotension.

frontHtml: First step for new orthostatic hypotension in an older adult on many drugs?
backHtml: Stop or reduce culprit drugs (α<sub>1</sub> blockers, diuretics, nitrates, tricyclics, sedatives).

frontHtml: Non-drug measures for orthostatic hypotension?
backHtml: 2–3 L fluid and liberal salt (if no HF/CKD), staged rising, compression stockings/abdominal binder, counter-manoeuvres, head-of-bed elevation, small meals, avoid alcohol and heat.

frontHtml: Drugs for persistent symptomatic orthostatic hypotension?
backHtml: Midodrine, droxidopa (neurogenic OH) or fludrocortisone; pyridostigmine for mild cases.

frontHtml: How is supine hypertension managed?
backHtml: Last pressor dose ≥ 4 hours before bed, head of bed raised, avoid lying flat by day, short-acting antihypertensive at bedtime only if needed.

frontHtml: Red flags that syncope is cardiac?
backHtml: Exertional or supine syncope, no prodrome, palpitations, structural heart disease, abnormal ECG, family history of sudden death.

frontHtml: Dietary advice for postprandial hypotension?
backHtml: Small, frequent meals lower in refined carbohydrate; avoid alcohol; water before meals.

frontHtml: Three triggers of renin release?
backHtml: Low renal perfusion pressure (afferent arteriole), β<sub>1</sub> sympathetic stimulation, low NaCl at the macula densa.

frontHtml: Why do ACE inhibitors cause cough and angioedema?
backHtml: ACE also degrades bradykinin; inhibition raises bradykinin.

frontHtml: Thiazide effects on serum calcium, uric acid and glucose?
backHtml: All tend to rise (hypercalcemia, hyperuricemia, hyperglycemia); potassium falls.

frontHtml: Hyaline vs hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis?
backHtml: Hyaline: benign hypertension/diabetes, pink homogeneous wall. Hyperplastic: malignant hypertension, onion-skin layers ± fibrinoid necrosis.

frontHtml: Primary vs renovascular hypertension: renin?
backHtml: Primary aldosteronism: renin low. Renovascular (and diuretics): renin high.

frontHtml: Why α before β blockade in pheochromocytoma?
backHtml: β blockade alone leaves α<sub>1</sub> vasoconstriction unopposed and can cause a hypertensive crisis.

frontHtml: Mechanism of amlodipine ankle edema?
backHtml: Arteriolar > venular dilation raises capillary hydrostatic pressure; diuretics barely help.

frontHtml: Hydralazine and minoxidil adverse effects?
backHtml: Hydralazine: reflex tachycardia, fluid retention, drug-induced lupus. Minoxidil: hypertrichosis, fluid retention, pericardial effusion.

frontHtml: Brain lesion of chronic hypertension that causes basal ganglia hemorrhage?
backHtml: Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms of the lenticulostriate arteries.

frontHtml: Blood pressure categories (adults)?
backHtml: Normal < 120/< 80; elevated 120–129/< 80; stage 1 130–139 or 80–89; stage 2 ≥ 140 or ≥ 90 mm Hg.

frontHtml: White-coat vs masked hypertension?
backHtml: White-coat: high in office, normal outside. Masked: normal in office, high outside (risk like sustained hypertension).

frontHtml: Usual blood pressure target for most adults?
backHtml: Below 130/80 mm Hg if tolerated.

frontHtml: Four first-line antihypertensive classes?
backHtml: Thiazide-type diuretic, ACE inhibitor, ARB, dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker.

frontHtml: Preferred antihypertensive with albuminuria?
backHtml: ACE inhibitor or ARB (never both).

frontHtml: Antihypertensives that are safe in pregnancy, and ones that are contraindicated?
backHtml: Safe: labetalol, extended-release nifedipine, methyldopa. Contraindicated: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, direct renin inhibitors.

frontHtml: Definition of resistant hypertension and the best fourth drug?
backHtml: Above goal on three classes including a diuretic (or needing four); spironolactone.

frontHtml: Lifestyle measures for hypertension?
backHtml: Weight loss, DASH-style diet, less sodium, more dietary potassium, exercise, limit alcohol.

frontHtml: Hypertensive emergency vs urgency?
backHtml: Emergency = severe hypertension with acute target-organ damage (ICU, IV drugs); urgency = no acute damage (oral drugs, follow-up).

frontHtml: How fast to lower pressure in most hypertensive emergencies?
backHtml: ≤ 25% fall in mean pressure in the first hour, then about 160/100–110 over 2–6 hours, then normal over 24–48 hours.

frontHtml: Aortic dissection blood pressure goal?
backHtml: β blocker first, then systolic about 120 mm Hg or lower within the first hour.

frontHtml: Fibromuscular dysplasia: patient, imaging, treatment?
backHtml: Woman under about 50; string-of-beads mid-distal renal artery; balloon angioplasty.

frontHtml: Screening test for pheochromocytoma?
backHtml: Plasma free (or 24-hour urine fractionated) metanephrines.

frontHtml: Toxicity of prolonged nitroprusside infusion?
backHtml: Cyanide (and thiocyanate) toxicity, especially with kidney failure.

frontHtml: Clues to coarctation as a cause of hypertension?
backHtml: Arm pressure higher than leg, weak delayed femoral pulses, rib notching.

frontHtml: Drugs that commonly raise blood pressure?
backHtml: NSAIDs, decongestants, stimulants, combined oral contraceptives, glucocorticoids, calcineurin inhibitors, VEGF inhibitors, licorice, alcohol.

frontHtml: Activator of lipoprotein lipase?
backHtml: Apolipoprotein C-II.

frontHtml: Apolipoprotein that mediates hepatic remnant uptake?
backHtml: ApoE.

frontHtml: What does PCSK9 do?
backHtml: Binds the LDL receptor and targets it for lysosomal degradation instead of recycling.

frontHtml: Familial hypercholesterolemia: gene and signs?
backHtml: Usually LDL receptor (autosomal dominant); tendon xanthomas, xanthelasma, premature arcus and coronary disease.

frontHtml: Familial chylomicronemia: defect and presentation?
backHtml: LPL or apoC-II deficiency (AR); pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis, creamy plasma layer.

frontHtml: Dysbetalipoproteinemia: genotype and signature xanthoma?
backHtml: ApoE2/E2 plus a second hit; palmar crease xanthomas.

frontHtml: Abetalipoproteinemia defect and complications?
backHtml: MTP deficiency; steatorrhea, acanthocytes, vitamin E deficiency ataxia and retinopathy.

frontHtml: Mechanisms: ezetimibe, bempedoic acid, fibrates?
backHtml: Ezetimibe blocks NPC1L1; bempedoic acid inhibits ATP-citrate lyase; fibrates activate PPAR-α (more LPL).

frontHtml: Lipid drug that raises triglyceride?
backHtml: Bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colestipol, colesevelam).

frontHtml: Fibrate adverse effects?
backHtml: Cholesterol gallstones; myopathy with statins (gemfibrozil worst).

frontHtml: Four statin benefit groups?
backHtml: Clinical ASCVD; LDL ≥ 190 mg/dL; diabetes aged 40–75; primary prevention 40–75 with elevated risk.

frontHtml: High-intensity statins and doses?
backHtml: Atorvastatin 40–80 mg, rosuvastatin 20–40 mg (≥ 50% LDL lowering).

frontHtml: Next steps when LDL stays above goal on a maximal statin?
backHtml: Add ezetimibe, then a PCSK9 inhibitor (or inclisiran).

frontHtml: Statin muscle aches with normal CK: management?
backHtml: Pause, then rechallenge at lower dose, different statin or alternate days; check TSH and interacting drugs.

frontHtml: Triglyceride level that calls for urgent lowering to prevent pancreatitis, and the drug?
backHtml: About ≥ 1,000 mg/dL; fibrate plus removal of secondary causes (alcohol, hyperglycemia).

frontHtml: Secondary causes of high LDL?
backHtml: Hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestatic liver disease, some drugs (glucocorticoids, cyclosporine, some progestins).

frontHtml: When is lipid screening done in children?
backHtml: Universally at about 9–11 and 17–21 years; earlier with family history of premature CVD or severe hypercholesterolemia.

frontHtml: Omega-3 product with event reduction in ASCVD with raised triglyceride on a statin?
backHtml: Icosapent ethyl (purified EPA).

frontHtml: Diet for familial chylomicronemia?
backHtml: Very low fat (about 10–15% of calories), medium-chain triglycerides, fat-soluble vitamin and essential fatty acid supplements.

frontHtml: Stanford type A vs type B aortic dissection: definition and usual treatment?
backHtml: Type A involves the ascending aorta → emergency surgery. Type B begins beyond the left subclavian and spares the ascending aorta → medical therapy (repair only if complicated).

frontHtml: Most common predisposing factor for aortic dissection?
backHtml: Chronic hypertension (others: Marfan, vascular Ehlers-Danlos, bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, Turner syndrome, stimulants, pregnancy, instrumentation).

frontHtml: Histology of the aortic media in Marfan syndrome or hypertensive ascending aneurysm?
backHtml: Cystic medial degeneration: fragmented, lost elastic fibers and pools of mucoid ground substance, with loss of smooth muscle cells.

frontHtml: Gene and protein in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome?
backHtml: COL3A1, type III collagen: spontaneous arterial, bowel and uterine rupture; thin translucent skin.

frontHtml: Mechanism of syphilitic aortitis?
backHtml: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum (plasma cells) → ischemic scarring of the outer media → ascending aorta/arch aneurysm, aortic regurgitation, 'tree-bark' intima.

frontHtml: Why does an aneurysm tend to keep growing (law of Laplace)?
backHtml: Wall tension ∝ pressure × radius; a wider segment carries more tension, so it stretches further.

frontHtml: Hoarseness with an aortic arch aneurysm: which nerve?
backHtml: Left recurrent laryngeal nerve, which loops under the arch by the ligamentum arteriosum.

frontHtml: Key process weakening the wall in abdominal aortic aneurysm?
backHtml: Transmural inflammation with matrix metalloproteinase degradation of elastin and collagen; smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor.

frontHtml: Suspected aortic dissection: imaging if stable vs unstable?
backHtml: Stable: CT angiography. Unstable: transesophageal echocardiography at the bedside or in the operating room.

frontHtml: Order of drugs in acute aortic dissection?
backHtml: Analgesia, then an IV beta-blocker (esmolol/labetalol) to heart rate ≈ 60/min, then a vasodilator if systolic pressure stays above about 120 mm Hg.

frontHtml: What makes a type B dissection 'complicated'?
backHtml: Malperfusion (gut, kidney, limb), rupture, rapid expansion, or refractory pain/hypertension → usually endovascular repair (TEVAR).

frontHtml: Who gets AAA screening, and how?
backHtml: One-time abdominal ultrasound in men aged 65–75 who have ever smoked.

frontHtml: Usual elective repair thresholds for abdominal aortic aneurysm?
backHtml: About 5.5 cm in men (about 5.0 cm in women), rapid growth (≈ 0.5 cm or more per year) or symptoms.

frontHtml: Pain, hypotension and pulsatile abdominal mass in an older smoker: next step?
backHtml: Ruptured AAA → straight to the operating room; permissive hypotension; no imaging if unstable.

frontHtml: Superior vena cava syndrome without a tissue diagnosis: why avoid empirical steroids or radiation?
backHtml: They can obscure the histology (especially lymphoma); give them only if airway compromise or cerebral edema forces urgent treatment (stent first).

frontHtml: Earliest visible lesion of atherosclerosis and its main cell?
backHtml: Fatty streak: intimal foam cells (macrophages that took up oxidized LDL through scavenger receptors).

frontHtml: Which cells make the fibrous cap of an atheroma, and what recruits them?
backHtml: Smooth muscle cells that migrate from the media into the intima, driven by growth factors such as PDGF.

frontHtml: Hyaline vs hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis?
backHtml: Hyaline: glassy plasma-protein/matrix thickening in chronic hypertension, diabetes, age. Hyperplastic: onion-skin smooth muscle layers in severe (malignant) hypertension.

frontHtml: Mönckeberg sclerosis: where, and what does it do to the ABI?
backHtml: Medial calcification of medium muscular arteries; lumen not narrowed; noncompressible vessels can give a falsely high ABI (> 1.40).

frontHtml: Cilostazol: mechanism and key contraindication?
backHtml: PDE3 inhibitor → ↑ cAMP → less platelet aggregation and arterial dilation; contraindicated in heart failure.

frontHtml: Why can clopidogrel fail in CYP2C19 poor metabolizers?
backHtml: Clopidogrel is a prodrug that CYP2C19 converts to the active P2Y<sub>12</sub> blocker; less activation means less platelet inhibition.

frontHtml: Young heavy smoker with digital ulcers, Raynaud and migratory superficial phlebitis?
backHtml: Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease); only complete tobacco cessation halts it.

frontHtml: Biopsy finding in cholesterol (atheroembolic) embolization?
backHtml: Biconvex, needle-shaped clefts in small arteries (cholesterol crystals dissolved in processing).

frontHtml: Fibromuscular dysplasia: who, which arteries, angiographic sign?
backHtml: Women aged 20–60; renal and internal carotid arteries; 'string of beads'; causes renovascular hypertension (high renin).

frontHtml: ABI cut-offs?
backHtml: ≤ 0.90 PAD; 0.91–0.99 borderline; 1.00–1.40 normal; > 1.40 noncompressible (do a toe-brachial index).

frontHtml: First-line therapy for intermittent claudication (after risk-factor control)?
backHtml: Supervised exercise program (about 3 sessions/week for at least 12 weeks); add cilostazol if still limiting and no heart failure.

frontHtml: Acute limb ischemia: first drug, then what?
backHtml: IV unfractionated heparin immediately; then revascularization according to viability (urgent if threatened, amputation if irreversible). Watch for compartment syndrome after reperfusion.

frontHtml: Define chronic limb-threatening ischemia and its management.
backHtml: Rest pain, non-healing ulcer or gangrene > 2 weeks → urgent imaging and revascularization for limb salvage.

frontHtml: Symptomatic carotid stenosis: who gets endarterectomy?
backHtml: TIA/non-disabling stroke in the territory with 70–99% stenosis (selected 50–69%), ideally within 2 weeks; not for occlusion.

frontHtml: Secondary Raynaud red flags and first test?
backHtml: Onset after ~40, asymmetry, digital ulcers, skin thickening, abnormal nailfold capillaries → ANA and nailfold capillaroscopy.

frontHtml: Chronic mesenteric ischemia: classic triad and test?
backHtml: Postprandial pain, food fear, weight loss in a smoker with vascular disease → CT angiography.

frontHtml: Three components of the Virchow triad, with one example each?
backHtml: Stasis (long travel, immobility), endothelial injury (surgery, catheter), hypercoagulability (cancer, estrogen, thrombophilia).

frontHtml: Factor V Leiden mechanism?
backHtml: Arg506Gln mutation removes the activated-protein-C cleavage site; factor Va resists inactivation.

frontHtml: Prothrombin G20210A?
backHtml: 3′ UTR variant of the prothrombin gene → higher prothrombin levels → venous thrombosis.

frontHtml: Heparin resistance with familial venous thrombosis suggests?
backHtml: Antithrombin deficiency (heparin acts through antithrombin).

frontHtml: Why is LMWH mainly anti-Xa?
backHtml: Its chains are mostly too short to bridge antithrombin and thrombin; Xa inhibition needs only antithrombin activation.

frontHtml: Warfarin skin necrosis: mechanism?
backHtml: Protein C (short half-life) falls before factors II, IX, X → transient hypercoagulability; risk ↑ with protein C deficiency; prevented by heparin overlap.

frontHtml: HIT pathogenesis and timing?
backHtml: IgG against heparin–PF4 complexes activates platelets via FcγRIIa → thrombocytopenia plus thrombosis, typically 5–10 days after starting heparin.

frontHtml: Reversal agents: dabigatran, apixaban/rivaroxaban, warfarin, heparin?
backHtml: Idarucizumab; andexanet alfa (or PCC); vitamin K + 4-factor PCC; protamine.

frontHtml: Brown skin above the medial malleolus in chronic venous insufficiency is due to?
backHtml: Hemosiderin from red cells leaking out of congested capillaries.

frontHtml: Trousseau syndrome?
backHtml: Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis from a cancer-associated hypercoagulable state, classically pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

frontHtml: Suspected DVT: test if unlikely vs likely (Wells)?
backHtml: Unlikely → high-sensitivity D-dimer (negative excludes). Likely → compression ultrasound.

frontHtml: Preferred anticoagulant for most patients with DVT?
backHtml: A DOAC (apixaban or rivaroxaban can be started without heparin lead-in). Exceptions: pregnancy (LMWH), antiphospholipid syndrome or mechanical valves (warfarin).

frontHtml: Duration of anticoagulation: provoked by surgery vs unprovoked?
backHtml: Major transient trigger → 3 months. Unprovoked or persistent risk (cancer) → at least 3 months, often extended if bleeding risk allows.

frontHtml: Indication for an IVC filter?
backHtml: Acute proximal DVT/PE when anticoagulation is contraindicated (e.g. active bleeding, recent intracranial hemorrhage); anticoagulate once safe.

frontHtml: Suspected HIT: what to do immediately?
backHtml: Stop all heparin (incl. LMWH, flushes) and start a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux or DOAC); no warfarin until platelets recover; no routine platelet transfusion.

frontHtml: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens?
backHtml: Massive iliofemoral DVT → swollen, painful, cyanotic leg with risk of venous gangrene → anticoagulation and urgent catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy.

frontHtml: Superficial vein thrombosis: when to anticoagulate?
backHtml: Leg segment ≥ 5 cm → prophylactic-dose anticoagulation (e.g. fondaparinux ~45 days); within ~3 cm of the saphenofemoral junction → treat as DVT; short arm segment → compresses and NSAIDs.

frontHtml: Venous ulcer treatment, and what to check first?
backHtml: Compression with elevation and wound care; check the ABI first because compression is unsafe with significant arterial disease.

frontHtml: Which cardiac chamber is most often injured by an anterior chest stab wound, and why?
backHtml: The right ventricle: it forms most of the anterior (sternocostal) surface.

frontHtml: Beck triad?
backHtml: Hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds: acute cardiac tamponade.

frontHtml: Mechanism of pulsus paradoxus in tamponade?
backHtml: Inspiration increases RV filling; with a fixed pericardial volume the septum bows left, reducing LV filling and stroke volume.

frontHtml: Hemodynamic hallmark of tamponade on right heart catheterisation?
backHtml: Raised, equalised diastolic pressures (RA ≈ RV diastolic ≈ PA diastolic ≈ wedge).

frontHtml: Where does blunt aortic injury usually occur, and why there?
backHtml: At the isthmus, just distal to the left subclavian at the ligamentum arteriosum: mobile arch meets tethered descending aorta.

frontHtml: Embryologic origin of the ligamentum arteriosum?
backHtml: Ductus arteriosus, from the left sixth pharyngeal arch artery.

frontHtml: Commotio cordis: mechanism?
backHtml: A low-energy chest blow during the upstroke of the T wave triggers ventricular fibrillation without structural injury.

frontHtml: Chest radiograph clues to traumatic aortic injury?
backHtml: Widened mediastinum, indistinct aortic knob, rightward tracheal or NG tube shift, depressed left mainstem bronchus, left apical cap, left hemothorax.

frontHtml: Tamponade versus tension pneumothorax at the bedside?
backHtml: Both: shock with distended neck veins. Tension: absent breath sounds on one side ± tracheal shift. Tamponade: equal breath sounds, muffled heart sounds.

frontHtml: Penetrating cardiac injury with tamponade and an available surgeon: treatment?
backHtml: Immediate operation (sternotomy or thoracotomy); pericardiocentesis only as a temporising bridge.

frontHtml: Strongest indication for resuscitative (ED) thoracotomy?
backHtml: Penetrating chest trauma with loss of pulses shortly before or after arrival (recent signs of life).

frontHtml: Screening for blunt cardiac injury?
backHtml: 12-lead ECG plus troponin; both normal excludes significant injury.

frontHtml: Blunt cardiac injury with new ECG changes but stable: management?
backHtml: Admit for continuous ECG monitoring (about 24–48 hours); echocardiography if unstable or unexplained arrhythmia.

frontHtml: Test of choice for suspected blunt aortic injury in a stable patient?
backHtml: CT angiography of the chest.

frontHtml: Anti-impulse therapy for a contained aortic injury: order of drugs?
backHtml: IV beta-blocker (esmolol) first to slow the heart, then a vasodilator if blood pressure stays high; withhold in hemorrhagic shock.

frontHtml: Preferred repair of blunt thoracic aortic injury?
backHtml: Thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR), after life-threatening hemorrhage elsewhere is controlled.

frontHtml: Young athlete collapses after a ball strikes the chest: first actions?
backHtml: Start chest compressions and defibrillate with an AED as soon as possible.

frontHtml: New hypotension and raised JVP after a pacing lead: suspect what, and what test?
backHtml: Ventricular perforation with tamponade; bedside echocardiography, then pericardiocentesis.

frontHtml: Adult derivative of the truncus arteriosus? Of the bulbus cordis?
backHtml: Truncus: ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk. Bulbus cordis: smooth outflow parts of both ventricles.

frontHtml: Adult derivatives of the left and right horns of the sinus venosus?
backHtml: Left horn: coronary sinus. Right horn: smooth posterior wall of the right atrium (sinus venarum).

frontHtml: Which cells form the aorticopulmonary septum, and which lesions follow their failure?
backHtml: Neural crest cells; truncus arteriosus (no septum), transposition (no spiral), tetralogy (malaligned outlet septum); linked to 22q11.2 deletion.

frontHtml: Why does the foramen ovale close at birth?
backHtml: Left atrial pressure rises above right atrial pressure (falling pulmonary resistance, more pulmonary venous return), pressing septum primum against septum secundum.

frontHtml: What keeps the fetal ductus arteriosus open, and what closes it after birth?
backHtml: Prostaglandin E<sub>2</sub> and low oxygen keep it open; rising oxygen and falling PGE<sub>2</sub> close it (→ ligamentum arteriosum).

frontHtml: Most oxygenated vessel in the fetus?
backHtml: Umbilical vein.

frontHtml: Eisenmenger syndrome: what reverses the shunt, and how do the murmur and P<sub>2</sub> change?
backHtml: Pulmonary vascular resistance exceeds systemic resistance; the original murmur softens and P<sub>2</sub> becomes loud.

frontHtml: Differential cyanosis (blue toes, pink fingers) suggests which lesion?
backHtml: PDA with reversed (Eisenmenger) flow entering the aorta distal to the left subclavian artery.

frontHtml: The four features of tetralogy of Fallot, and their single embryologic cause?
backHtml: RV outflow obstruction, malaligned VSD, overriding aorta, RV hypertrophy; anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum.

frontHtml: Why does squatting help a child with tetralogy of Fallot?
backHtml: It raises systemic vascular resistance, reducing right-to-left shunting and increasing pulmonary blood flow.

frontHtml: Transposition of the great arteries: CXR sign and maternal association?
backHtml: Egg-shaped heart with a narrow mediastinum; maternal pregestational diabetes.

frontHtml: Most characteristic heart defect in Down syndrome, and its embryologic origin?
backHtml: Atrioventricular septal defect; failure of the endocardial cushions.

frontHtml: Coarctation: four exam findings?
backHtml: Arm hypertension, weak delayed femoral pulses (low leg pressure), interscapular murmur, rib notching; associated with Turner syndrome and bicuspid aortic valve.

frontHtml: Infant at 1–3 months with sweating during feeds and Q waves in I, aVL, V5–V6?
backHtml: Anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ischemia as pulmonary pressure falls).

frontHtml: Cardiac lesion of Williams syndrome? Of Noonan syndrome?
backHtml: Williams: supravalvular aortic stenosis. Noonan: pulmonary valve stenosis (and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy).

frontHtml: Cyanotic newborn whose saturation does not rise with 100% oxygen: first drug?
backHtml: Alprostadil (PGE<sub>1</sub>) infusion; watch for apnea.

frontHtml: Tet spell management sequence?
backHtml: Calm, knee-to-chest, oxygen → IV fluids, morphine → beta-blocker → phenylephrine; avoid inotropes.

frontHtml: Shock with weak femoral pulses in the first 2 weeks of life: think of what, and give what?
backHtml: Duct-dependent systemic lesion (critical coarctation, interrupted arch, hypoplastic left heart); start alprostadil.

frontHtml: Small asymptomatic muscular VSD with normal growth: management?
backHtml: Reassurance and follow-up; many close spontaneously; no endocarditis prophylaxis.

frontHtml: Drugs to close a significant PDA in a preterm infant, and contraindications?
backHtml: Ibuprofen or indomethacin (or acetaminophen); avoid NSAIDs with bleeding, thrombocytopenia, NEC or significant renal impairment.

frontHtml: Definitive operation for transposition of the great arteries?
backHtml: Arterial switch operation in the first weeks of life (balloon atrial septostomy before it if mixing is poor).

frontHtml: Secundum ASD with right heart enlargement and normal pulmonary resistance: treatment?
backHtml: Transcatheter device closure (surgery for primum, sinus venosus or unsuitable rims).

frontHtml: When is PFO closure recommended?
backHtml: Adults up to about 60 years with a nonlacunar cryptogenic ischemic stroke and a PFO, especially with a large shunt or atrial septal aneurysm, after other causes are excluded; plus antiplatelet therapy.

frontHtml: Key counselling point for a woman with Eisenmenger syndrome?
backHtml: Pregnancy carries very high maternal mortality and is advised against; avoid estrogen-containing contraception.

frontHtml: Which congenital heart patients need dental endocarditis prophylaxis?
backHtml: Unrepaired cyanotic disease (incl. shunts/conduits), first 6 months after repair with prosthetic material, residual defect at prosthetic material; also prosthetic valves, prior endocarditis, transplant valvulopathy.

frontHtml: Late problems after repair of tetralogy of Fallot?
backHtml: Pulmonary regurgitation with RV dilation, ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death; pulmonary valve replacement for symptoms or progressive dilation.

frontHtml: Anthracycline cardiotoxicity: pattern, mechanism, protection?
backHtml: Cumulative dose–dependent dilated cardiomyopathy (topoisomerase IIβ, iron-mediated free radicals), largely irreversible; dexrazoxane reduces risk.

frontHtml: Trastuzumab cardiotoxicity: mechanism and reversibility?
backHtml: HER2 (ERBB2) signalling blockade in cardiomyocytes → dysfunction without much necrosis; not dose-dependent, usually reversible.

frontHtml: Chemotherapy that causes coronary vasospasm?
backHtml: 5-Fluorouracil and capecitabine.

frontHtml: Cancer drugs causing myocarditis?
backHtml: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (often with myositis/myasthenia); high-dose cyclophosphamide (hemorrhagic myocarditis).

frontHtml: How does cocaine cause myocardial ischemia?
backHtml: Blocks NE/DA/5-HT reuptake → α<sub>1</sub> coronary vasoconstriction + ↑ demand (β<sub>1</sub>) + thrombosis.

frontHtml: Why can cocaine widen the QRS?
backHtml: It blocks fast Na<sup>+</sup> channels; treat with IV sodium bicarbonate.

frontHtml: ACE inhibitor cough and angioedema: mediator?
backHtml: Bradykinin (and substance P), because ACE = kininase II; not IgE-mediated.

frontHtml: Why does amlodipine edema not respond to diuretics?
backHtml: It comes from precapillary arteriolar dilation (↑ capillary hydrostatic pressure), not salt retention.

frontHtml: Minoxidil: mechanism and adverse effects?
backHtml: Opens K<sub>ATP</sub> channels in arteriolar smooth muscle; hypertrichosis, fluid retention, reflex tachycardia, pericardial effusion.

frontHtml: First-dose syncope: which antihypertensive class?
backHtml: α<sub>1</sub> blockers (prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin).

frontHtml: Digoxin toxicity: classic symptoms and arrhythmias?
backHtml: Nausea, confusion, yellow-green vision; PVCs, bidirectional VT, atrial tachycardia with block, AV block; hyperkalemia in acute overdose.

frontHtml: Drugs that raise digoxin levels via P-glycoprotein?
backHtml: Amiodarone, verapamil, quinidine, clarithromycin.

frontHtml: Electrolyte disturbances that increase digoxin toxicity?
backHtml: Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia (and renal failure).

frontHtml: Before anthracycline or trastuzumab therapy?
backHtml: Baseline echocardiogram (LVEF) and risk-factor optimization.

frontHtml: Asymptomatic EF fall ≥ 10 points to < 50% on trastuzumab?
backHtml: Hold trastuzumab, start HF therapy, reimage in about 3–4 weeks; often restart if it recovers.

frontHtml: Cocaine chest pain: first-line drug class and class to avoid?
backHtml: Benzodiazepines (with aspirin, nitrates, CCB); avoid β-blockers during acute intoxication.

frontHtml: After ACE inhibitor angioedema, which drugs are contraindicated?
backHtml: All ACE inhibitors and sacubitril-valsartan; ARBs only with caution.

frontHtml: ACE inhibitor cough in a patient with albuminuria?
backHtml: Switch to an ARB.

frontHtml: Acceptable creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor?
backHtml: Up to about 30%; larger rises suggest volume depletion or renal artery stenosis.

frontHtml: Indications for digoxin-specific antibody fragments?
backHtml: Life-threatening arrhythmia, hemodynamic instability, end-organ dysfunction, or high K<sup>+</sup> in acute ingestion.

frontHtml: Is digoxin removed by hemodialysis?
backHtml: No: large volume of distribution.

frontHtml: Amlodipine-induced ankle edema: best fix?
backHtml: Lower the dose and/or add an ACE inhibitor or ARB.

frontHtml: QTc threshold to avoid adding another QT-prolonging drug?
backHtml: About 500 ms (or a rise of more than about 60 ms).

frontHtml: Verapamil or diltiazem plus a β-blocker: main risk?
backHtml: Additive bradycardia and AV block, especially in older adults.
